verdict: Avoid new fertiliser exposure in Kakinada for now; lend only to deregulated, non-subsidy specialty/customised players with clean receivables, and decline subsidy-dependent units and traders.
title: Kakinada Fertilisers: a note to the credit manager
narrative:
## What this business physically is
**Fertiliser making here is a gas-and-acid conversion business: ammonia, phosphoric acid and sulphuric acid go in, urea and complex granules come out, and cash comes back through either the market or a subsidy claim.** The value sits in two very different places: commodity urea/complex is price-controlled and subsidy-fed, while customised and specialty products are sold on agronomy and service and are far less regulated [8]. **So when a proposal lands, first ask what share of revenue is subsidy-linked versus deregulated; if subsidy is above half, ask for the last three subsidy-claim ageing statements before anything else.**

## Where cash and value sit
**Working capital is the whole game: inventory of acid and finished stock, plus a receivables tail that is either dealer credit or a government claim.** Peer results show the split clearly: Shree Pushkar's chemical segment grew 38.1% year-on-year while its fertiliser segment revenue fell 10.6% [4], and Deepak Fertilisers' margins rose from 16.8% to 21% on chemicals even as fertiliser-linked revenue receded [7]. **So check the receivables mix line by line; if more than a third is subsidy or government claim, ask for the sanction and disbursement trail on the last two claims.** Capex is lumpy and acid-storage heavy; collect from customer the project cost and debt-equity before sizing any term loan.

## What has changed now
**The local signal is negative and it is specific: the NFCL unit in Kakinada has closed, and the Ramagundam plant in Telangana is not meeting Andhra Pradesh's demand, which has intensified the urea shortage for farmers [3].** That source is dated and reads as roughly a year old, so treat it as context, not current fact. The data pack is unambiguous: Andhra Pradesh GST collections are -0.2% Apr-to-date against India +6.1% [D], and India-wide fertiliser output (NIC 20) is -0.5% YoY and -1.2% Apr-to-date [D]. **Bank credit to the sector is running +53.1% YoY against that -1.2% output [D], so when a proposal lands, check whether the loan is funding stock or funding a gap; if drawing power is being met by fresh limits, ask why.**

## Where to grow, and how to grow safely
**Pursue the deregulated end: customised and specialty fertiliser makers, water-soluble and bio-stimulant blenders, and dealers with genuine agronomy service and year-round sales across seasons [8].** The structural demand story is real: complex fertiliser capacity is set to add around 4 million tonne per annum through fiscal 2029 over a base of ~16 MTPA [9]. **Avoid subsidy-claim-dependent urea units, single-product traders, and anyone whose cash flow depends on a plant restart at Kakinada.** Structure as cash-flow-backed working capital with a drawing power tied to paid stock and clean receivables, and take monthly stock-and-receivable statements, monthly GST returns, and quarterly subsidy-claim status.

## Early-warning signs
**Watch the receivable ageing and the claim cycle, not the topline.** If dealer credit days stretch beyond the stated terms, or a subsidy claim ages past its normal cycle, cut the limit before the next season. If GST turnover for the borrower diverges from the state's -0.2% trend [D] in a way the books cannot explain, ask for the sales register. If a borrower's chemical or specialty share is shrinking toward commodity fertiliser, reprice or exit.
watch: Monthly GST returns and stock statement
Turnover falls two months running or stock is unsupported by invoices -> freeze fresh drawings and inspect godown
Subsidy or government claim ages beyond normal cycle -> move to cash-collateralised limit
Claim rejected or held -> ask for revised cash flow and re-size limit
Dealer credit days exceed agreed terms -> cut limit before the season
Any restart or new local capacity announced -> reassess borrower's pricing and volume assumptions
